sound.text: Magnum Opus took about a year, and at 18 songs it's the longest project SyWavy and Jett2Fly have made. It swings between moods from one song to the next, hard rap beats against slow R&B, and Jett2Fly's synths run under nearly all of it. Vertex opens on real drum sounds and a heavy bass guitar, Steer rides a walking upright bass, and SZA and Tower of Tears are built on live guitar. Flame sounds like it samples an old doo-wop record, but the voices are Jett2Fly's own, shifted lower. The Part Time Models play the distorted guitar on Put It On!, and a Vine boom is hidden very quietly under the hits on Awtside.

notes.title: Genie in a Bottle
notes.body: Christina Aguilera's 1999 debut single, whose hook is about being rubbed the right way. The rubbing comes first, then the genie.

ref.name: Genie in a Bottle (Christina Aguilera song)

notes.title: Emerson
notes.body: A member of The Part Time Models, who's in the Put It On! video.
Magnum Opus starts here, and the title says where it starts: a vertex is the highest point, the tip of the curve. The opening lines are about getting the room moving before he says anything else.

notes.title: CeeLo Green
notes.body: The Atlanta singer from Goodie Mob and Gnarls Barkley. The line turns his name around so the color comes first, and the green carries over to the Athletics, the baseball team that played across the bay from San Francisco in Oakland, in green and gold.

notes.title: Dsquared2
notes.body: The fashion label run out of Milan by Canadian twin brothers Dean and Dan Caten. He shrugs it off as everyday wear.

notes.title: Magic Johnson
notes.body: The Lakers great, his name split across the line. Magic follows the genie she wants, and Johnson is slang for what she grabs.
Right after skipping safe sex, he needs a plan, and the next line lands on B. Plan B is the morning-after pill.

notes.title: Pilot G2
notes.body: The gel pen from Japan's Pilot, known for how smoothly it writes. A poet's ink glides out of a G2, and the next line takes off as a G6.

notes.title: Like a G6
notes.body: Far East Movement's 2010 hit, named for a Gulfstream private jet. The G2 pen turns into the G6 jet right after a Jett2Fly ad-lib, and flight is the running image for his producer's name.

ref.name: Like a G6 (Far East Movement song)

notes.body: He treats the verse like pottery, fired until it's hard enough to last, then puts the song's name up in the sky like an ad. It's the album's opener announcing itself.

notes.title: Rowdy Rebel
notes.body: The Brooklyn artist from Bobby Shmurda's GS9 crew. His name is split across these two lines.

notes.title: Turks and Caicos Islands
notes.body: The Caribbean islands southeast of the Bahamas, a getaway spot. The name also rhymes with closing a case.

notes.title: Rihanna
notes.body: The Barbados-born singer. The line names two of her albums back to back, from 2009 and 2011.

notes.title: Barbados
notes.body: Rihanna's home island in the eastern Caribbean. He borrows her albums and her accent in one line.

notes.title: Nicolas Cage
notes.body: Nic is short for nicotine, so the actor's name turns into a vape he keeps hitting for days. Cage also played Ghost Rider, whose head is a skull on fire, and that's the flaming head in the next line.

notes.title: Runtz
notes.body: A popular weed strain named after Runts, the fruit candy. Poppin can mean doing well, and it's also what you do with candy.

notes.title: Erykah Badu
notes.body: The Dallas singer who led neo-soul with her 1997 album Baduizm. The line borrows the title of her first single, and she sets up the OutKast song that follows, which André 3000 wrote about their breakup and her mother.

notes.title: Ms. Jackson
notes.body: OutKast's 2000 hit, André 3000's apology to the mother of his ex, the singer named two lines earlier.
Three times the outro repeats the OutKast apology, and the last time he takes the apology back entirely. The album's first song ends on a smirk instead of a sorry.

Rust is trust with the T worn off, and the song keeps trading one for the other. It's the slow damage that forms when something is left out too long, and that's how he sees a love that's been neglected.
The bridge bends the words people say at funerals by changing one letter. He refuses to sit still and corrode, and he can't rest while it's happening.

notes.title: Deadstock
notes.body: Sneaker and resale slang for old stock that was never sold or worn, still new in the box. His trust is just that, and the rusted love after it is trusted love missing its T.

notes.title: Hannah Montana
notes.body: The Disney Channel show about a girl living a double life as a pop star, played by Miley Cyrus. Its theme song is The Best of Both Worlds, and his two worlds are two women.
He opens on defense. Accused of cheating, he denies it and asks for proof. Then he turns it around: two women on his phone, as permanent as the ink on his arm.

notes.title: Palm Angels
notes.body: The streetwear label Francesco Ragazzi started in Milan in 2015. A brand named for angels should come with working wings, and he says these don't, so he's out.
Breaking ankles is basketball talk for a crossover so quick the defender falls. She's up in heels that high and still won't go down for his moves.

notes.title: Plan B
notes.body: The morning-after pill. Cycle means a bad habit to the first woman and a period to the second, and the pill shows up right after.
A diet joke. She'd better eat meat, while he's the vegan who smokes his greens and still gets cheese, the money kind.
The bridge drops the bragging for something closer to thanks. Each woman changed him: one by showing him the warning signs, the other by showing him a bigger life.

notes.title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
notes.body: Steven Spielberg's 1982 film about a stranded alien who just wants to call his planet. The line turns that famous plea into asking her to bring him home.

notes.title: Dior
notes.body: The French fashion house, whose menswear line was long called Dior Homme. The line trades that for a home of his own.

notes.title: Batman
notes.body: DC's caped hero, known as the world's greatest detective. Even he didn't find out, which is the point right after hiding the evidence in the car.
The ending cracks the bravado. He insists he never cheated, says the hurt is all coming from her, and wonders out loud whether better even exists.

notes.title: Shannon Sharpe
notes.body: The Hall of Fame tight end turned TV host, whose personal life became headline news in 2024 and 2025. He closes by saying he won't play that role.

notes.title: Good Days
notes.body: SZA's 2020 single about holding on to hope after a love ends. The hook opens on its title and puts those days in the past.

notes.title: Snooze
notes.body: SZA's 2022 hit from SOS about never wanting to miss a minute with someone. He wishes he could press it on the breakup instead.

The verse runs through everything this relationship has a hold on, and nothing is left out, which suits a song named for the singer whose debut album is Ctrl. He knows they're bad for each other and still can't end it, which is all the hook says.

notes.title: Broken Clocks
notes.body: A 2017 single from SZA's Ctrl about time moving on while she looks back. Here it's a moment with her that stopped time.

From here to the end of the bridge, nearly every line is built from SZA song titles out of Ctrl (2017), its 2022 deluxe edition, and SOS (2022). He tells the story of this relationship in her words, the same way the song borrows her name.

notes.title: 2AM and Tread Carefully
notes.body: Two songs from SZA's vault that she added to Ctrl's deluxe edition for its fifth anniversary in 2022. The bridge opens on both of them.

notes.title: Love Galore
notes.body: Ctrl's 2017 single with Travis Scott, about wanting more from someone who keeps it casual. Miles, in the same line, is another song from Ctrl's deluxe edition.

notes.title: Wavy (Interlude)
notes.body: A short Ctrl track featuring James Fauntleroy. Its title is half his name, so he slips himself into her album.

notes.title: Prom
notes.body: A Ctrl song about not being ready to grow up, paired with the school night he says he never had. Anything, at the end of the line, is another Ctrl song.

notes.title: Supermodel
notes.body: The song that opens Ctrl, an open letter to someone who left her feeling like she wasn't enough.

notes.title: Drew Barrymore
notes.body: Ctrl's lead single, named for the actor, about feeling out of place and wanting to be wanted. Normal Girl, also on Ctrl, ends the line, flipped to say she isn't one.

notes.title: Go Gina
notes.body: A Ctrl song about letting loose and refusing to be held back, chanted here like a cheer.

notes.title: Pretty Little Birds
notes.body: A slow Ctrl track featuring Isaiah Rashad, and one more title in the run.

notes.title: SOS
notes.body: SZA's 2022 album, named for the distress signal. The line spells out the phrase those letters are often said to stand for.

notes.title: Love Language
notes.body: An SOS song about learning how to love someone the way they need. The line folds another SOS title in right before it.

notes.title: Used
notes.body: An SOS track featuring Don Toliver, tucked into the start of the line.

notes.title: Gone Girl
notes.body: An SOS song about needing space and still wanting to be held onto. The line pairs it with another SOS title and repeats it like a plea.

notes.title: SZA
notes.body: Solána Rowe, the St. Louis-born, New Jersey-raised R&B singer behind Ctrl and SOS. The song is named for her and built from her catalog, and the last line asks someone to be that kind of friend to him.
Heal sounds like heel, and Carolina Herrera is known for heels: its Good Girl perfume comes in a bottle shaped like a stiletto. Cat makes it a dirty joke too.

notes.title: Carolina Herrera
notes.body: The Venezuelan-born designer and the New York fashion house she built, also known for perfumes like Good Girl. Later he splits the name around spraying it, a nod to the fragrances.

notes.title: Saddam Hussein
notes.body: Iraq's leader from 1979 to 2003. Hussein rhymes with insane, and Usain does it again in the next line.

notes.title: Usain Bolt
notes.body: The Jamaican sprinter who holds the world records in the 100 and 200 meters. The line runs his name backward, and it leads straight into the Jamaican run that follows.

notes.title: Jamaican Patois
notes.body: The English-based language spoken across Jamaica, which dancehall carried around the world.

notes.title: Jamaica
notes.body: The Caribbean island nation. He says he isn't from there, but its listeners treat him like he is.

notes.title: Popcaan
notes.body: The Jamaican dancehall star of the Unruly crew, later signed to Drake's OVO Sound. Being embraced like him is the compliment.

notes.title: Kevin Durant
notes.body: The scoring star who spent his first nine seasons with the Sonics and Thunder, then left for Golden State in 2016 without a title in Oklahoma City. That sets up the next two lines.

notes.title: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander
notes.body: The Canadian guard who became the Thunder's star after Durant, and in 2025 won league MVP and the team's first title in Oklahoma City. His first name sounds like shy.

notes.title: Oklahoma City Thunder
notes.body: The NBA team that won the 2025 championship. Paired with the sprinter from earlier in the verse, it makes lightning.

notes.title: Facebook
notes.body: Face and book, two lines apart, make Facebook, and the poke was its old button for nudging someone. Getting booked is also what follows a case.

notes.title: Pope Leo XIV
notes.body: Robert Prevost, elected in May 2025 as the first pope from the United States, was born in Chicago. He says he isn't from there, and the next line says where he is from.

notes.title: St. Petersburg, Florida
notes.body: His city, known locally as the Burg, which he reps with his friends.

notes.title: Martin Luther King Jr.
notes.body: The civil rights leader whose 1963 speech at the March on Washington is remembered for its dream. Here it's Jett2Fly sharing a dream for their music.

notes.title: Better Call Saul
notes.body: The Breaking Bad spinoff (2015 to 2022) about the lawyer Saul Goodman. The line turns telling her to go call someone else into the show's title.

notes.title: Tigger
notes.body: The bouncing tiger from Winnie the Pooh, a fair picture of how he moves on a beat.
He points back to Wavy Life, his 2023 album about water, freedom and coming home grown, and says he's living it now. Three years on, it isn't just an album title to him anymore.

notes.title: Pink Tape
notes.body: Lil Uzi Vert's 2023 album. Spinning it again works as a dance move and as playing the record one more time.

The song ends on Jett2Fly. His beats sound like a pair of jets taking off, which fits a producer whose name is about flying. Earlier, the song credits Jett with dreaming big for the music the two of them make together.

notes.title: Treasure
notes.body: A nod to Bruno Mars's 2013 single Treasure, a song that calls a girl exactly that.
The title gets its answer in the hook: he won't ease off a love he expected to keep for life. He's tried everything to set it right, and she still won't give.
Cursed means swearing in the first line and doomed in the next ones. He watched his language for her, then goes back and forth on whether they're jinxed.

By now the hurt shows up even in a smile. He knows her well enough to see the tears coming, and the last line runs his own name into the slang for crying, so the waves and the tears are the same water.
The relationship becomes a car that won't start, and he keeps pushing it anyway. Exhaust works two ways here, the fumes and how tired he is. He still believes it can be fixed.

notes.title: The Foreign Exchange
notes.body: The R&B duo of the singer Phonte and the Dutch producer Nicolay, who made their first album trading files online before they ever met. It works the plain way too, as foreign money.

notes.title: Kawasaki
notes.body: The Japanese motorcycle maker. The song opens on a rival bike before settling on Yamaha, and every ride in it means two things.

notes.title: Indianapolis 500
notes.body: The century-old Memorial Day weekend race, 200 laps around the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. He treats the night like a race.
Zack Snyder's film with Gerard Butler as the Spartan king Leonidas. The line names the actor and the movie together.

notes.title: Stevie Wonder
notes.body: The Motown great, a keyboard player first. The line flips his name around and leads with keys, which is also the name of SyWavy's 2020 single, Keys'. Dreams adds a second Stevie: it's Stevie Nicks's 1977 hit with Fleetwood Mac.

notes.title: Isn't She Lovely
notes.body: Stevie Wonder's 1976 song for his newborn daughter, from Songs in the Key of Life. That album title ties back to the keys in the line before.

notes.title: Peyton Manning
notes.body: The Hall of Fame quarterback, famous for shouting Omaha at the line to change the play. The call also rhymes into Yamaha.

notes.title: Yamaha
notes.body: The Japanese name on motorcycles and on pianos and keyboards. The song rides both meanings: the bike and the keys.

notes.title: Helmut Lang
notes.body: The Austrian designer and his minimal label, a 1990s favorite. On a song about bikes, his first name turns into a helmet.
The ride turns into a band: drums to beat, strings to play. Yamaha makes those too, so the hook's double meaning moves from the bike to the instruments.

notes.title: Bunraku
notes.body: Traditional Japanese puppet theater from Osaka, where the puppeteers work in plain sight. It shows up right after strings, next to a bit of French.

notes.title: Wendy Wu: Homecoming Warrior
notes.body: The 2006 Disney Channel movie with Brenda Song as a teen who learns she's a destined warrior. The next line takes the warrior straight to basketball.

notes.title: Golden State Warriors
notes.body: The Bay Area team whose dynasty won four titles in eight years. He says that story is over.

notes.title: Klay Thompson
notes.body: The Warriors sharpshooter who won all four of those titles and left for the Dallas Mavericks in 2024. His name stands in for play.

notes.title: Dallas Mavericks
notes.body: Klay Thompson's team after he left Golden State, which is why the Mavs come right after him.

notes.title: Soulja Boy
notes.body: The artist whose 2008 hit with Sammie was about kissing over the phone. The ringing in the next lines answers it.

Keys' is SyWavy's March 2020 single, his first record with Jett2Fly. The song keeps saying it has put miles on, and with Yamaha making keyboards, the ride and the record turn into one image. Here he claims it outright, down to the year.

Low brass is what a band calls its tubas and other deep horns, and SyWavy played the tuba in school band before high school. It's the last of the music he says he's made himself, after keys and rapping. Yamaha makes tubas too.

notes.title: Jeff Bezos
notes.body: Amazon's founder, and his name stands for money here. Prime Student is Amazon's cheaper plan for college students, and two-day shipping is what made Prime famous, so these lines all run through his company.

notes.title: Line 6
notes.body: The California maker of guitar amps and effects, one more piece of music gear in a song built on Yamaha's double life.

notes.title: Mercedes-Benz
notes.body: The German luxury carmaker. Amends, said quickly, ends in a Benz, and he'd still take the Yamaha, bike or keyboard, over one.

notes.title: Dapper Dan
notes.body: The Harlem tailor who remade luxury logos for hip-hop stars in the 1980s and now works with Gucci. He sets his Florida style apart from the Harlem original's.

notes.title: Bella Thorne
notes.body: The Shake It Up actress has talked since she was a kid about her dyslexia, and how her brain mixed up letters like b and d. Disney even wrote it into an episode of the show. That's why the mixed signals, right after the dyslexia line, land on her.

notes.title: Wallah
notes.body: Arabic for I swear to God. Closing the verse with it, he swears every word is true.
The hook owns everything. Shameless here means he admits his mistakes out loud instead of hiding them, even though the verse later says he isn't proud of it.

notes.title: The Goonies
notes.body: The 1985 adventure film about kids hunting for pirate treasure. He bends its name, then borrows Sloth's famous shout to the kids to get people streaming his music.

notes.title: Netflix
notes.body: Flix is Netflix, and the line is the Netflix and chill joke: a movie's on, and nobody's watching it.
A varsity jacket is also called a letterman jacket, and dyslexia mixes up letters, so both halves of the line turn on letters.

notes.title: Nevel Papperman
notes.body: The rival kid on Nickelodeon's iCarly, always scheming from behind a computer. Calling someone a Nevel makes him a petty schemer chasing money through a screen.
He watches every front give way, one per line, until even the truth turns out to be an act.
The outro is everyone weighing in. He's tired of the commentary, and the song ends with him telling shame itself to be quiet.

notes.title: Los Angeles Sparks
notes.body: The WNBA team, right before the Indiana Fever. Spark is also lighting up.

notes.title: LiAngelo Ball
notes.body: The middle Ball brother, who goes by Gelo. Jell-O sounds just like it, keeping the run of Ball brothers going, and his 2025 song Tweaker is what got him moving as an artist.
The opening is a bowling joke. He needs her PIN to get in and her pin to knock down, while someone with slow hands has been rolling for two hours, a ball in the joke and a blunt in real life.
The hook hangs on one word with two meanings. Proceeds are the money a sale brings in, and to proceed is to keep going. He spends, she dances, and the money and the night both keep moving.

notes.title: Nike
notes.body: The sportswear giant, named for the Greek goddess of victory, right after he compares his build to Greek myth. Its swoosh is a check mark, which is how checking becomes Nike.

notes.title: The Dark Side of the Moon
notes.body: Pink Floyd's 1973 album. One word is swapped so the line points at smoke instead of the moon.

ref.name: The Dark Side of the Moon (Pink Floyd album)

notes.title: Caitlin Clark
notes.body: The record-setting guard who went from Iowa to the WNBA's Indiana Fever in 2024. Catching a fever means catching her team.

notes.title: LaVar Ball
notes.body: The outspoken father of NBA players Lonzo and LaMelo Ball. Ball is the family name, and raising sons is his claim to fame, which turns into a boast about treating rivals like his kids.

notes.title: LaMelo Ball
notes.body: The youngest Ball brother, a Charlotte Hornets star. Mellow sounds like his name.

notes.title: Lonzo Ball
notes.body: The oldest Ball brother. The Lakers drafted him in 2017 and he later played for the Chicago Bulls, so these two lines trace his career.

notes.title: Mighty Morphin Power Rangers
notes.body: The 1990s kids' show where teenagers team up and combine their machines into one giant robot. Uniting is the whole point.
California stands for its wildfires here, the kind that burned through Los Angeles in January 2025. Burning woods sets it up.
A T break is a tolerance break, time off from weed so it hits harder later. Right off the bat it makes him rabid, and bats are known for carrying rabies.

notes.title: Tom Hanks
notes.body: The two-time Oscar-winning actor. T. Hanks is his name and thanks at the same time, so the line says both.

notes.title: The Green Mile
notes.body: The 1999 prison drama starring Tom Hanks, which drew four Oscar nominations. Green has its other meaning here too, and the Academy, the group that hands out the Oscars, comes right after.
Three five, Q and zip are weed amounts: 3.5 grams, or an eighth, then a quarter ounce and a full ounce. Woods are Backwoods, the cigars people roll blunts in, and he's trying to stop burning them.
The hook asks for a straight answer: who showed her the best time, and where does he stand now. He can't read anything between them, so he needs her to say it.

notes.title: Anne Hathaway
notes.body: The Oscar-winning actor from Les Misérables. Her last name sounds like having to wait, and her 2024 romance comes in the next line.

notes.title: The Idea of You
notes.body: Anne Hathaway's 2024 Prime Video romance, about a single mom who falls for a younger boy band singer. The title becomes someone he's holding out for.

notes.title: The Sweet Escape
notes.body: Gwen Stefani's 2006 hit with Akon, which leads into the lines about her.

notes.title: Gwen Stefani
notes.body: The singer who fronted No Doubt before her solo career. Her first name sounds like went.

notes.title: No Doubt
notes.body: Gwen Stefani's band from Anaheim, California, whose 1995 breakout single finishes the line.
The song ends on a choice. Someone changed him, and he says he'd put her ahead of the habits he's been leaning on.

notes.title: The O
notes.body: Orlando's nickname, and the Magic are its NBA team. He waves off the team and the city in one line.

notes.title: Dolce & Gabbana
notes.body: The Milan fashion house known by its initials, sunglasses included.

notes.title: Deal or No Deal
notes.body: The Howie Mandel game show built on choosing briefcases, with a million dollars at the top. It starts a run of million-dollar names.

notes.title: Slumdog Millionaire
notes.body: Danny Boyle's 2008 Best Picture winner about a Mumbai teen on a TV quiz show. The line splits its title, right after another million-dollar game show.

notes.title: Roy Jones Jr.
notes.body: The boxing great who won world titles from middleweight all the way up to heavyweight. He sets himself next to a fighter who kept moving up.

notes.title: VLONE
notes.body: The streetwear label from the A$AP Mob circle, known for its big orange V. Its name comes from its motto about living and dying alone, which answers the end of the line before.

notes.title: Paco Rabanne Invictus
notes.body: Paco Rabanne's 2013 men's fragrance, named for the Latin word for unconquered. He wears the word the way he wears the scent.

notes.title: Michael Jackson
notes.body: The King of Pop. The lines take the title of his 1979 album and his backward glide across the stage, in the black loafers he danced in.

notes.title: Black Clover
notes.body: The anime and manga about Asta, a boy born with no magic in a world that runs on it. That's why the next line shrugs magic off.

notes.title: St. Petersburg, Florida
notes.body: His city, known locally as the Burg. He's headed there because it's on the rise.
The hook is about betrayal. Someone crossed a line he'd never cross, and it showed him who they really are.

notes.title: Time Warner
notes.body: The media giant that became WarnerMedia after AT&T bought it in 2018, while its cable arm became Spectrum. A company that changed its name, like the person in the line.

notes.title: Tom Joyner
notes.body: The radio host whose Tom Joyner Morning Show ran on Black radio for 25 years, until 2019. A morning conversation calls up his name.

notes.title: Pop Warner
notes.body: The national youth football league, named for coach Glenn Pop Warner. A sack counts on the field and off it.

notes.title: Warner Bros.
notes.body: Bro and Warner in one line make Warner Bros., the Hollywood studio, one more Warner in the run.

notes.title: Tijuana
notes.body: The Mexican border city, with the juana from marijuana in it, right after rolling up. Rolling flats also makes it Tijuana Flats, the Tex-Mex chain that started in Florida.

notes.title: Juwanna Mann
notes.body: The 2002 comedy about a suspended NBA player who poses as a woman to play in a women's league. She wants to make films, just not that one.

notes.title: Nirvana
notes.body: The Washington band that led grunge in the early 1990s. Spirit points to their biggest hit, Smells Like Teen Spirit, and nirvana is also the Buddhist word for release from suffering.

notes.title: Kurt Cobain
notes.body: Nirvana's singer and songwriter, the face of 1990s grunge. The next lines dig into his band's biggest album.

notes.title: In Bloom
notes.body: A Nirvana song from Nevermind (1991). Drain You, from the same album, is in the line too.

notes.title: Nevermind
notes.body: Nirvana's 1991 album, the one with the baby swimming after a dollar on the cover. He uses its title to brush her off.

notes.title: Knives Out
notes.body: Rian Johnson's 2019 murder mystery, paired with a dinner pun. It starts the film talk that closes the song.
The song closes on his other craft. He directs, and the final word blends his name with cinema, a signature for the films he makes.
A straight love song. In his eyes she was his partner from the start, and a ring wouldn't change anything that was already true.
He asks to hold the moment still like a paused shot, a film term from someone who directs his own videos.
The outro is about responsibility. He takes on keeping her safe, the way he loves her, even how she looks, and owning all of it is how he shows he's serious.
The 25th is his birthday, December 25.

notes.title: Bow Wow
notes.body: Byron is Bow Wow's character in Tyler Perry's Madea's Big Happy Family (2011), and Lottery Ticket is the 2010 comedy he starred in, about a kid who wins the lottery. Two of his movies, back to back.
A wreck and erect sound almost the same, so the crash in one line turns into a sex joke in the next.
His mind is the car in this verse, running on its own and a little twisted. All he wants is her relaxed and along for the ride.

notes.title: Vine
notes.body: Twitter's six-second video app, shut down in 2017. Six seconds is also how long he lasted with her, which is the joke.

notes.title: Young Dolph
notes.body: The Memphis artist who built his own label, Paper Route Empire, and stayed independent. His name works as a verb here, and with M.I.A., Miami's airport code, in front of it, the line spells out the Miami Dolphins.

notes.title: Passenger princess
notes.body: Internet slang for a partner who always rides up front while someone else drives.

notes.title: NASCAR
notes.body: American stock car racing, run out of Daytona Beach, Florida, home of the Daytona 500. It fits a song about steering.

notes.title: Ralph Lauren
notes.body: The American fashion house, welded here to a denim label to make one name.

notes.title: True Religion
notes.body: The Los Angeles denim brand known for the horseshoe stitching on its back pockets. It's the other half of the blend.
Steer and stir sound almost alike, and the song uses both. Someone is stirring up trouble, and he takes control of the car to swerve away from it.

notes.title: Empire
notes.body: Fox's drama about the Lyon family and the record label they fight over, which ran from 2015 to 2020.

notes.title: The Twilight Zone Tower of Terror
notes.body: The elevator drop ride at Disney's Hollywood Studios, part of Walt Disney World in Florida. The title trades its terror for tears, and the elevator a few lines later rides the same shaft.

ref.name: The Twilight Zone Tower of Terror

notes.body: Love here is an elevator, rising and dropping, and she stands taller than everything he's afraid of. He gave things up for her, and he hasn't moved since.

notes.title: Pink + White
notes.body: A song from Frank Ocean's 2016 album Blonde, its colors flipped here.

notes.title: Blonde
notes.body: Frank Ocean's 2016 album, the one the line before borrows from. Here it's something only the two of them share.
The bridge is memory slipping. He's losing hold of what her touch felt like, and he can't get the tears out on his own.

notes.title: Rapunzel
notes.body: The Brothers Grimm fairy tale about a girl locked in a tower who lets down her long hair. On a song built on towers, it's the way up.

notes.title: Tangled
notes.body: Disney's 2010 animated take on Rapunzel. The title becomes wanting the two of them wrapped up together.

notes.title: Nav and Lil Uzi Vert
notes.body: Two artists named side by side, and Leaders is a song the two of them made together.

notes.title: Pinocchio
notes.body: The puppet whose nose grows whenever he lies, and who dreams of being a real boy. In bed, where they lie, something grows, and he swears it's real.

notes.title: Sade
notes.body: The British band fronted by Sade Adu, whose smooth 1980s and 1990s records set the standard for late-night R&B. Her name lands in a hazy line about hope.

notes.title: Desert Eagle
notes.body: The heavy pistol known as the Deagle, made famous by movies and games like Counter-Strike. In this song, it's his name for her.

notes.title: Bill Gates
notes.body: Microsoft's co-founder. The lines split his name: the gates he hopes his friends reach, then no bill.

notes.title: Mitski
notes.body: The Japanese American singer-songwriter behind raw indie songs like Nobody. Her name sets up the rhyme.

notes.title: St. Petersburg, Florida
notes.body: His city, known locally as the Burg, which he's making his own through the songs.
2028 is the next presidential election, and runner works both ways: running for office, and the song that keeps running on every playlist.

He names the album here, in a single that came out in July 2025, ten months before Magnum Opus did. A magnum opus is an artist's greatest work, and the word also belongs to Magnum Research, the company behind the Desert Eagle, which ties the album's title to this song.
He calls out his own double meanings, and the verse ends by sending whatever jams back to the sea, home ground for someone named Wavy.
Bars are verses and the playground kind, so after the monkey bars he asks her to swing over.

notes.title: KP & Envyi
notes.body: The R&B duo behind the 1998 hit Shorty (You Keep Playin' with My Mind). He reaches for late-90s R&B as a mood.

notes.title: Mase
notes.body: The Harlem artist whose 1997 debut Harlem World made him Bad Boy Records' breakout star. He wants that run without the label's founder.

notes.title: Sean John
notes.body: The clothing line Sean Combs started in 1998. After Combs's 2024 arrest, he wants no part of it and dresses his own way.

notes.title: Tony Hawk
notes.body: The skater whose name is on the Pro Skater video games. Gliding over a beat becomes a grind down a rail.
The hook holds two things at once: real hurt, and someone who still lights him up. Even after she disappointed him, the spark is hers.
The bridge plays like an interrogation. He asks why she left and who she's with now, and tags each one as a question still waiting for an answer.
Moving on isn't happening, and neither is lighting up for anyone else. So he waits, asking her not to disappoint him again.

notes.title: John Gotti
notes.body: The New York mob boss, nicknamed the Dapper Don for his expensive suits. Being the freshest on Gotti means dressing like him.

notes.title: Rick Owens
notes.body: The California-born designer known for dark, draped clothes and sculpted sneakers. She wants his look head to toe.

notes.title: Takashi Murakami
notes.body: The Japanese artist behind the smiling flowers, the cover of Kanye West's Graduation and years of Louis Vuitton bags. A tidal wave of his work suits someone named Wavy.

notes.title: Thrift Shop
notes.body: The hook of Macklemore and Ryan Lewis's 2012 hit about buying secondhand clothes, a fit for a song full of vintage pieces. Za is slang for weed.

notes.title: Prada
notes.body: The Milan fashion house, here a bag he hands over. Said fast, the name and the word after it sound like proud of you.

notes.title: Cam'ron
notes.body: The Harlem artist who led the Diplomats, or Dipset, and whose pink mink at New York Fashion Week in 2002 became a style landmark. His name doubles as come on.

The Part Time Models' singer takes this part and steps into the closet. She raids it before he's done with a piece, vintage tees included, and getting dressed is treated as art, worth more than most people earn.
The hook is the compliment he keeps hearing. The title means getting dressed and pulling it off at the same time.

notes.title: Comme des Garçons
notes.body: Rei Kawakubo's Tokyo label, a pillar of experimental fashion. She wants the clothes but won't show love for the music.

notes.title: Back to the Future
notes.body: The 1985 time-travel classic. Switching outfits through the decades is his time machine.

notes.title: Jordan Poole
notes.body: The NBA guard who won a title with the Golden State Warriors in 2022. A pool gets you wetter, and Poole spells it his way.

notes.title: FUBU
notes.body: The streetwear label Daymond John and his friends started in Queens in 1992. Its name stands for For Us, By Us.

notes.title: Benihana
notes.body: The Japanese steakhouse chain where the chef chops and cooks at your table. Chopping it up is also slang for talking.
Thrax is a weed strain, and sticky hands come from breaking down the good stuff.

notes.title: Ben Roethlisberger
notes.body: The Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback who won two Super Bowls. Stealing sounds like Steelers, which is how he gets into the line.

notes.title: Vetements
notes.body: The Paris label known for oversized fits and logo jokes, founded by Demna in 2014. It's the fit he comes back in.
Lion sounds like lyin', so Wave never lies, and the Maine right before it sounds like a lion's mane.

notes.title: Dennis Rodman
notes.body: The Hall of Fame rebounder as famous for his piercings, tattoos and dyed hair as for his five titles. He wants the look to match.

notes.title: The Curious Case of Benjamin Button
notes.body: The 2008 film where Brad Pitt ages backward. Something getting old is the opposite of Button, and the name hands off to money in the next line.

ref.name: The Curious Case of Benjamin Button

notes.title: Benjamin Franklin
notes.body: Benjamins are $100 bills, which carry Franklin's face, so the Button line turns into money. Frankly, on the next line, finishes his name.
Awtside is outside spelled the way he says it, and being outside means being out, seen and in demand. The hook keeps him there, with a crowd that keeps asking for more.

notes.title: Martin Lawrence
notes.body: The comedian behind the 1990s sitcom Martin. He starred with Eddie Murphy in the 1999 comedy Life, which the line slips in.

notes.title: Eddie Murphy
notes.body: The comedy star of Coming to America. The title turns into a sex joke, and the bib sets up his day care movie in the next line.

notes.title: Daddy Day Care
notes.body: Eddie Murphy's 2003 comedy about laid-off dads who open a day care. It plays off the line about not having a kid.

notes.title: Denim Tears
notes.body: Tremaine Emory's label, known for jeans printed with cotton wreaths that speak to Black American history. Too many jeans sounds like too many genes.
He traces his path: he came up rapping, then added singing, and now he does both. Then the moment that proves it: at his shows, the crowd answers back when he calls out Wave.

notes.title: Bloomingdale's
notes.body: The New York department store, part of a closet he talks about like home.

notes.title: Polo Bear
notes.body: Ralph Lauren's teddy bear mascot, knit into its sweaters since 1991.

notes.title: Floyd Mayweather Jr.
notes.body: The boxer who retired undefeated at 50 and 0. The weather in the line before finishes his name.

notes.title: PETA
notes.body: People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, the group that campaigns against leather and fur. He wears it anyway.

ref.name: People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals
